gap.evidence: the need for enhanced catalyst durability and regeneration strategies
gap.reason: The introduction motivates improved automotive catalyst materials that maintain high activity under low-temperature and transient conditions, resist degradation over vehicle lifetimes, and reduce platinum-group-metal consumption.

source_text:
Mobile sources such as automobiles account for a significant portion of atmospheric emissions of harmful pollutants. At the 27th Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP27), 41 countries agreed under the Accelerating to Zero Coalition (A2Z) framework to sell only zero-emission vehicles—electric and fuel-cell vehicles—by 2035 in leading markets and by 2040 world-wide.1,2

Nevertheless, the automotive industry anticipates that conventional internal-combustion-engine (ICE) vehicles will continue to occupy a non-negligible market share for the foreseeable future. Accordingly, emission regulations for gasoline and hybrid vehicles (HEVs) are expected to become increasingly stringent so as to ensure clean exhaust even under transient and low-temperature conditions.3–5 This tightening of global regulations has accelerated the development of advanced after-treatment technologies, including high-efficiency three-way catalysts (TWCs), electrically heated catalysts, and integrated exhaust-energy-management systems.3 In Europe, the transition from Euro 6 to Euro 7 represents a major milestone, imposing stricter limits on NOx, particle number, and non-methane hydrocarbons while also mandating catalyst durability throughout vehicle lifetime.4 Moreover, real-driving-emission (RDE) studies have revealed a degradation of gasoline-vehicle performance with increasing mileage, emphasising the need for enhanced catalyst durability and regeneration strategies.5 Thus, even in the era of rapid electrification, the progressive reinforcement of emission standards for hybrid and gasoline engines remains a key driving force for innovation in catalyst materials and reaction-mechanistic research.

To achieve both high catalytic activity and reduced consumption of platinum-group metals (PGMs), recent research on automotive catalysts has focused on multi-element alloy catalyst design based on the control of the electronic state of active metals.6,7 For instance, tuning the density of states (DOS) in Cu–Ni alloys can optimise adsorption energies and realize lower temperature oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons without using PGMs.8 Similarly, Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu alloys have been reported to suppress poisoning by H2O and NO while enabling CO and hydrocarbon oxidation at temperatures below 150 °C.9–11 Beyond binary and ternary alloys, multi-element alloy catalysts that exploit both electronic-structure diversity and configurational-entropy effects have emerged as a new framework capable of simultaneously achieving high activity, thermal stability, and PGM saving. A representative example is the high-entropy alloy (HEA), which contains multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios.12–15 HEAs possess high configurational entropy and tuneable electronic structures, providing catalytic functions that are unobtainable with conventional alloys.

queries.broad: For automotive exhaust catalysts, what single intervention could improve catalytic activity and durability while reducing platinum-group-metal consumption? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.
queries.problem_constrained: Starting from a multi-element automotive alloy catalyst containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios, what single intervention could overcome activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption during transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation, including exposure to H2O and NO and degradation associated with thermal aging or increasing mileage? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the untreated starting catalyst, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.
queries.expert_context: Automotive-catalyst studies have used electronic-state control in multi-element alloys to combine activity with reduced platinum-group-metal consumption. Reported Cu–Ni alloys tuned the density of states to improve CO and hydrocarbon oxidation at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu alloys suppressed H2O and NO poisoning and enabled oxidation below 150 °C. High-entropy alloys containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been investigated because configurational entropy and tunable electronic structures may support activity, thermal stability, and platinum-group-metal saving. However, increasingly stringent regulations require clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation as well as durability over vehicle lifetime, and real-driving-emission studies show performance degradation with mileage. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis giving the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted change relative to the unmodified catalyst, the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose result could falsify it.

leaks.why: Points toward element-specific electronic redistribution as the route by which the catalyst’s activity and resistance to poisoning may be improved.
Identifies an electronic-structure mediator closely related to the answer’s post-ageing electronic reconstruction of multimetal sites.
Directs attention to electronic structure as the relevant mediator rather than purely particle size, sintering, or composition.
